title: The Last Lantern Anew
premise: In the winter of 1848, in the river city of Vellmar, Mirabel Vane cuts type in her late father's print shop, convinced that revolutions are ink for other people's newspapers. When a frightened child, Odile, is left at the door with a note reading 'forget the face,' Mirabel and the shop's ragtag household — an exiled typesetter, a runaway compositor, and her father's old foreman — are drawn into printing a banned pamphlet that could sway whether the armistice is signed or the city burns. As soldiers close in and loyalties fracture, Mirabel discovers the child is the granddaughter of the general whose signature the pamphlet must sway, and that 'forget the face' was a plea to erase a dangerous likeness. In the final days before the armistice, the household completes the print run as the shop is put to the torch; Mirabel saves the type, the child, and the truth, choosing found family over the father's legacy — and signs the last pamphlet with her own name.
about_author: Isandro Galloway is the pen name of a former letterpress restorer who spent a decade cataloguing nineteenth-century print shops before turning to fiction. They write historical novels about ordinary tradespeople caught in extraordinary politics, and live near a decommissioned paper mill.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Letters
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. A day in the Vane print shop: cutting type, minding accounts, deflecting the foreman Bram's worries about the growing unrest in Vellmar. Mirabel insists history happens elsewhere. Emotional beat: quiet denial, the comfort of routine before it shatters.

chapters.title: A Child at the Door
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. On a freezing night, a knock reveals Odile, seven years old, clutching a note: 'forget the face.' No name, no claimant. The household debates turning her over to the constabulary. Emotional beat: reluctant tenderness; Mirabel's first crack in her detachment.

chapters.title: The House That Ink Built
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV rotating through the household — exiled typesetter Corvin, runaway compositor Sef, foreman Bram. Each remembers how they came to the shop. Emotional beat: the shop revealed as a haven of the displaced; found family established as fragile, unspoken.

chapters.title: What the Constable Knows
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. A city constable makes 'routine inquiries' about a missing child of 'a certain family.' Mirabel lies for the first time in her life and doesn't know why. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into protectiveness; the stakes become personal.

chapters.title: Corvin's Bag of Type
chapters.summary: Corvin's POV. He reveals a hidden cache of type and a banned pamphlet draft — 'The Lantern Anew' — arguing the armistice must not be signed until the general answers for the massacres. He asks the shop to print it. Emotional beat: the moral fork; Corvin's guilt over a betrayal in his exile.

chapters.title: The Face in the Locket
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She finds a locket sewn into Odile's coat: a miniature portrait of the general — and of a woman who looks like Odile. 'Forget the face' means destroy the likeness. Emotional beat: dread; the child is not random, she is evidence.

chapters.title: Sef's Night Run
chapters.summary: Sef's POV. Sent to a sympathetic bookseller for paper, Sef witnesses a barricade going up and a boy shot in the street. He returns changed, silent, and begins sleeping in the shop's cellar. Emotional beat: the revolution stops being rumor; grief and adrenaline.

chapters.title: Bram Refuses
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The old foreman refuses to print the pamphlet — the shop was the father's life, and soldiers hang printers. His argument with Mirabel exposes her buried resentment of the father who left her the shop instead of a childhood. Emotional beat: family fracture; power of legacy as a chain.

chapters.title: The General's Men
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. An officer in civilian dress visits, asking after a girl with 'family features,' offering coin. Mirabel realizes Odile's grandfather is the general whose signature the armistice needs — and whose crimes the pamphlet names. Emotional beat: temptation and clarity; she sends him away.

chapters.title: Setting the Argument
chapters.summary: Corvin and Sef's shared POV. The household begins setting type in shifts at night, Odile learning letters at the stone. Bram watches from the stairs, not helping, not stopping them. Emotional beat: purpose crystallizing; the shop becomes a workshop of resistance.

chapters.title: Odile Asks About Her Mother
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Odile reveals fragments: her mother fled the general's house, hid with printers, was caught. Mirabel understands the note was the mother's last instruction — and that the mother may be alive in a military prison. Emotional beat: Mirabel's denial fully collapses; she commits.

chapters.title: The First Proof
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The first proof sheet comes off the press; it is beautiful and damning. Bram finally puts his hands on the press, wordlessly joining. Emotional beat: found family sealed in ink; brief, luminous hope.

chapters.title: Cordon
chapters.summary: Sef's POV. Soldiers seal the river quarter after a printing house is raided; the bookseller is arrested. The household must decide whether to distribute or destroy the run. Corvin argues distribution; Bram argues survival. Emotional beat: claustrophobia; time running out before the armistice.

chapters.title: The Bargain with the Bookseller's Widow
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Mirabel trades the widow safe passage out of the city for a distribution network. It means using Odile's likeness as proof of the general's hidden family — weaponizing the child's face. Emotional beat: corruption of good intent; power's first taste of Mirabel.

chapters.title: What Corvin Did in Exile
chapters.summary: Corvin's POV. Confession: he informed on his own press circle years ago to save his skin; the mother of Odile was among those he betrayed. The household's trust fractures. Emotional beat: guilt made flesh; the question of whether people are their worst act.

chapters.title: The Armistice Table
chapters.summary: Interlude from the perspective of a clerk at the armistice negotiations, reading a smuggled proof of 'The Lantern Anew.' The delegates waver; the general demands the printers' heads. Emotional beat: the shop's work echoing in halls of power; dread and vertiginous significance.

chapters.title: Raid
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Soldiers come at dawn. The household hides Odile in the type cabinet's false back; Bram holds the door and is taken. The press is smashed; the shop's heart broken. Emotional beat: terror, sacrifice, the cost made real.

chapters.title: The Last Form
chapters.summary: Corvin and Sef's POV. In the cellar, with salvaged type, they set the final pamphlet by candlelight — Mirabel's addition: the mother's account of the general's crimes, in her own words. Emotional beat: resolve forged in ruin; printing as resurrection.

chapters.title: Forget the Face
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Mirabel must decide: use Odile's face to force the general's hand, or honor the mother's note and let the child be no one's evidence. She burns the locket portrait, keeping only the mother's testimony. Emotional beat: renouncing power's corrupt shortcut; identity chosen, not imposed.

chapters.title: The Night of Lanterns
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The pamphlets flood the city; lanterns appear in windows in solidarity. Soldiers are ordered to burn the quarter but hesitate as crowds gather. Odile, carried on Sef's shoulders, is one face among thousands — unremarkable, safe. Emotional beat: climax; the crowd as the true press.

chapters.title: Armistice
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The armistice is signed — with the general's resignation attached. Bram is returned in a prisoner exchange, changed but alive. The shop is a shell; the household surveys the ashes and the salvaged type. Emotional beat: exhausted, imperfect victory; grief and gratitude entwined.

chapters.title: Anew
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, epilogue. Spring. The household reopens as 'Vane & Household, Printers,' with Odile's name set in type for the first time — hers, not her grandfather's. Mirabel signs the shop's first new broadside with her own hand. Emotional beat: resolution; history no longer happens to other people — she makes it.
